title: Seven runs and a spring
hook: Hajar runs seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, and water springs by the baby's feet

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hajar in the valley, asking the one question that mattered. Your line was then we will not be lost. Did you set one worry down, even for an hour? Day forty.

To the door and back. To the door and back. A parent pacing a hallway at three in the morning, because moving is the only thing left to do. That's where we find Hajar. The dates are gone. The water skin is empty. She is thirsty, the baby is thirsty, and Isma'il is crying and twisting on the ground. She can't bear to watch. So she climbs the nearest hill and looks for anyone at all. Nobody. She runs down, across the valley floor, and up the hill on the other side. Nobody. Today's word is what she found.
screen: `THE WATER SKIN IS EMPTY.` → `SHE CLIMBS AND LOOKS.` → `NOBODY.`

segments.voice: The same hadith in Bukhari tells it. The first hill is Safa. The second is Marwa. She goes back and forth between them seven times, climbing, looking, running the low stretch between. On the seventh, she hears a voice. She says, you've made me hear you; if you can help, help. And there, by the baby, is an angel, striking the ground with his heel, and water comes up out of the dry earth. She hurries to hold it in, scooping sand around it into a little basin, filling her skin. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, telling this story long afterward, adds a line of pure tenderness: may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il. If she had left it alone, Zamzam would have been a flowing stream. That spring is Zamzam, and it still flows in Mecca, in the grounds of the great mosque, where pilgrims drink from it and carry it home in bottles for the people who couldn't come. Where the name comes from, nobody knows for certain. A story people tell says Hajar called out zam, zam, hold still, gather, as she held the water in. Take that as a story, not a record. And the running didn't stop with her. The Prophet said that's why people go between the two hills. Pilgrims at Hajj and Umrah walk between Safa and Marwa seven times, and in one marked stretch the walk quickens, as hers did. The Qur'an calls Safa and Marwa among the signs of Allah. So a rite of the pilgrimage retraces a mother's search. Not her calm, her running. It honors the searching as much as the finding.
screen: `SAFA TO MARWA, SEVEN TIMES.` · `WATER FROM THE DRY GROUND.` · `IF SHE HAD LEFT IT, A STREAM.` · `PILGRIMS WALK HER WALK.` · then, large: `ZAMZAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk it. If there's room where you are, stand up and take seven steps one way, then seven back. Seven times, if you can, slowly. If you can't stand, trace it with a finger on your knee. With each length, think of one thing you're still looking for, still hoping for, still running toward. If you pray, you can make a small prayer on each length. If not, just count, and feel your feet. The bell holds the time.
Zamzam. The spring that came up by Isma'il's feet in the dry valley, still flowing in Mecca today. Today's word.
Your line: keep running; the water comes. When today makes you pace, let the pacing count as part of the search, not a failure of it. Day forty.

howItsDone: During Hajj and Umrah, pilgrims walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, a rite called sa'y, and drink Zamzam water, which pilgrims often carry home to share with family and friends.

fork.setup: you're Hajar. water suddenly springs up by the baby's feet in the dry valley. what do you do?
options: let it run and fill the valley.
hold it in with sand and fill your water skin.
run to the hill to call for help.
fork.reveal: she scooped sand around it to keep it. the Prophet ﷺ said, with tenderness, that if she'd left it, Zamzam would have been a flowing stream.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the spring in Mecca. its origin is uncertain; one story links it to "zam," hold still, gather.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy well in Mecca.
what it means: the spring that came up in the dry valley after Hajar's seventh run between Safa and Marwa.
what a scholar hears: the story is in Bukhari, told by the Prophet ﷺ; the rite of sa'y between the hills keeps it, and the Qur'an calls the hills signs of Allah (2:158).

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 (Hajar's search, the angel and the spring)
Qur'an 2:158 (Safa and Marwa among the signs of Allah)

notes: Details from Bukhari 3364 (from memory): seven runs, the voice, the angel striking the ground with his heel (some versions: his wing), Hajar hemming the water in, and the Prophet's words 'may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il; had she left it, Zamzam would have been a flowing spring.' Please confirm number and paraphrase.
The angel is identified as Jibril in some narrations; the script says only 'an angel'.
Origin of the name Zamzam: presented explicitly as uncertain, with 'zam zam' as a story people tell. Confirm this framing.
"In a marked stretch many hurry": in sa'y men traditionally hasten between the green markers; women usually walk. Stated as 'many hurry' to avoid a ruling; confirm.
Practice outline says 'walk back and forth seven steps, praying'; adapted to seven lengths of seven steps, with prayer offered as optional.

Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer tells the listener what they know and drops 'her milk has dried up' (the hadith says the water ran out and she and the baby grew thirsty); 'every pilgrim', 'many hurry' and 'one of the central rites of Islam' softened; Zamzam placed 'in the grounds' of the mosque rather than the courtyard. Confirm the Bukhari 3364 details.
